paragraphs: The following judgments concern media technical directors/managers' daily work coordinating technical departments such as camera, editing, engineering, and maintenance to produce radio/television programs; they do not predict hiring, qualifications, broadcast permissions, or ultimate responsibility.

Media technical directors/managers (O*NET27-2012.05) coordinate camera, editing, engineering, and maintenance departments to produce radio and television programs, test equipment, switch video sources, monitor pictures and broadcasts, and liaise between engineering and production. Specific control, content, and site safety responsibilities require verification against organizational authorization and applicable rules.

60-minute paper exercise (all inputs fictional; no real equipment operation or broadcasting): program-relative time is 00:00—30:00. The script specifies C1 host wide shot for 00:00—10:00, C2 guest close-up for 10:00—20:00, and P1 short video for 20:00—30:00. Use a hard cut at 10:00 and a 2-second dissolve at 20:00; the dissolve belongs to the third segment and adds no time. Equipment list: C1/C2 cameras, P1 player, switcher S, and monitor M. Precheck records: C1 picture normal, C2 no signal, P1 picture normal, S selection test normal, M display normal. Exercise rules: switch only to sources confirmed normal and permitted. Permissions for C1 and C2 are confirmed; P1 permission awaits the responsible person's confirmation. Do not alter the script independently. Record anomalies first and submit them to the production lead for decisions. Write a planned switching table, an available/pending table, and two escalation questions. Write conditional branches following approval without assuming permissions have been resolved or equipment restored. Spend the first 10 minutes reading, 25 minutes making tables, 15 minutes independently reviewing, and 10 minutes writing corrections and unresolved questions. These internal rules are neither law nor real equipment test procedures.

Reference solution (hide before answering independently): the three planned segments are each 10 minutes, 10+10+10=30. The 10:00 hard cut to C2 is currently unexecutable because C2 has no signal. The 20:00 switch to P1 is currently unexecutable because permission is pending. Only C1 meets the exercise's normal-and-permitted conditions. Do not independently fill all 30 minutes with C1 or mark C2/P1 as broadcast-ready. Submit C2's missing signal and P1's pending permission separately to the production lead, retaining both plans and actual states. If the lead confirms C2 is restored and P1 permission is valid, follow the approved script with a hard cut at 10:00 and a 2-second dissolve starting at 20:00; the third segment remains 20:00—30:00. The work sample includes the plan, five equipment prechecks, source permission states, two anomalies and conditional branches, and one correction. Paper reasoning cannot prove equipment safety, field competence, or broadcast authorization.

This page covers O*NET 27-2012.05, Media Technical Directors/Managers: coordinating technical departments such as camera, editing, engineering, and maintenance to produce radio/television programs. Common reported titles include Broadcast Director, News Technical Director, Newscast Director, Operations Director, Production Director, Production Manager, Studio Director, and Technical Director. This page excludes adjacent occupations such as Project Management Specialists, Computer Systems Analysts, and Network and Computer Systems Administrators.

entries: Inputs: studio and production equipment, camera and switching signals, program scripts and production instructions, station or network policies and regulations, editing and studio facility schedules, and broadcast and safety conditions requiring confirmation.

Verifiable outputs: equipment test and status records, switching and effects execution records, broadcast monitoring and compliance records, facility schedules, training records, and fault handling and handover records.

Complete workflow: test equipment and check signals → arrange camera positions and switching according to the script → execute switches and effects → monitor broadcasts and check policy compliance → coordinate engineering and production departments → record, review, and hand over, completing the loop.

paragraphs: Key judgments: whether equipment and signals are normal; whether switching meets script and live requirements; whether broadcast content complies with station or network policies and regulations; whether site and equipment safety conditions are met; and whether commitments involving minors or guest contracts fall within authorization.

US O*NET survey: 100% use email daily, 94% have constant contact with others, 86% face time pressure daily, 81% consider accuracy extremely important, 81% work in controlled indoor environments daily, 94% use telephones daily, 79% have face-to-face discussions daily, and 77% usually work more than 40 hours a week. These are respondent percentages, not Chinese working hours or employer guarantees.

Research inputs: O*NET27-2012.05 identity, tasks, context, ECR, and education concern the suboccupation; 2025 wages, 2025—2035 employment, and industries concern parent occupation Producers and Directors (27-2012). US broadcast policy task context is not extrapolated to Chinese rules, qualifications, or industries.

Verify first: equipment and signal states, program scripts and switching requirements, station or network policies and regulations, studio and editing facility availability, site equipment safety conditions, and technical, content, and safety judgments requiring an authorized person's confirmation.

Work cycle: begin with equipment testing and script checks, proceed through camera positioning, switching and effects execution, broadcast monitoring and compliance checks, and end with department coordination, records, and handover. Do not use untested equipment, broadcast content before policy checks, or proceed before safety or compliance questions are confirmed.

Adjacent responsibility boundaries: this page covers only radio/television technical control and production coordination under 27-2012.05. Project management specialists focus on project schedules and risks; computer systems analysts focus on information system proposals; network and computer systems administrators focus on system operations. Their objects of work, authorization, and responsibilities are not interchangeable.

Difference from project management specialists: project management specialists coordinate project schedules, budgets, and risks; this occupation handles field execution and switching for radio/television technical control and production.

Difference from computer systems analysts: computer systems analysts focus on information system requirements and solution design; this occupation focuses on studio and broadcast technical control equipment and signal processing.

Difference from computer network support specialists: computer network support specialists handle network and endpoint troubleshooting support; this occupation handles technical control of camera, switching, monitoring, and broadcast signal chains.

Difference from network and computer systems administrators: these administrators handle servers, networks, and account operations; this occupation focuses on studio technical control and live production equipment and signals. Compare outputs and authorization.
Tasks and AI: media technical directors/managers' task exposure to AI does not equal job replacement. Humans remain responsible for broadcast switching, content compliance, and equipment safety.

Editorial trial suggestion: use only fictional scripts and status records to try AI-assisted log organization, switching-table drafts, and lead retrieval. Check durations, actual states, and permissions individually. O*NET recruitment technology directories do not prove adoption of these GenAI tasks. Tools cannot issue permissions, repair equipment, or replace organizational authorization. AI Impact Score 42% is an editorial estimate. Parent occupation 27-2012: 181,000 employed in 2025, projected 188,300 in 2035, growth of 4% over 2025—2035 and a net increase of 7,300; 12,100 average annual openings include replacements. Employment includes self-employed people, while OEWS wages exclude them; these cannot be treated as the same wage sample. Parent-occupation figures are not separate occupational figures.

How to interpret these figures: explain employment levels, growth rates, net changes, and annual openings separately; they cannot be combined into an individual employment guarantee. Combined scope cannot replace a separately reported occupation. Industry and regional differences are substantial; do not extrapolate across regions.
Fit signals: assess media technical director/manager fit through observable behavior, without substituting personality labels for tasks, qualifications, and responsibility judgments.

Direct answer: if you can follow procedures for switching, testing, and compliance checks under live broadcast pressure and accept responsibility for broadcast results, further exploration is worthwhile. Otherwise, compare adjacent directions first.

Positive signals: making explainable technical and switching judgments under time-slot and live broadcast pressure, willingness to coordinate engineering and production, and accepting responsibility for broadcast results.

Reasons for caution: if responsibility for broadcast and equipment results is difficult or you lack patience for high-pressure live broadcasts and frequent coordination, consider adjacent directions or engineering roles first.
Trial action: complete a technical control, testing, and compliance exercise using entirely fictional studio switching, then decide whether to continue.

RIASEC (ECR): the interest code describes preferences for leadership and decisions (Enterprising), procedural equipment and record handling (Conventional), and operating physical equipment (Realistic). Use it only to generate hypotheses, not infer hiring or competence.

Editorial self-check: separately check three 10-minute segments, the 2-second dissolve adding no time, C2's missing signal, and P1's pending permission; retain one correction. These behaviors explore accuracy and recording habits. Big Five labels do not predict hiring or authorization.
Labels such as MBTI cannot determine competence. First check actual tasks, standards, and responsibility boundaries, then decide whether to continue.

Switching or signal errors: failing to check signals and instructions under procedures when switching may cause broadcast interruptions and complaints. Controls include procedural checks and retained records. Boundaries depend on broadcast policies and employers.
Using equipment before testing: failure to test under procedures before equipment use may cause downtime or safety problems. Test under procedures and confirm status.

Broadcast content violating policies or regulations: content that violates station or network policies and regulations may cause compliance problems. Monitor and record under policies and regulations.

Unconfirmed remote live-broadcast site conditions: remote work without confirming site safety conditions may injure people or damage equipment. Confirm conditions under site safety procedures before working.

Common escalation rule: whenever equipment, content, site safety, or contract applicability is unclear, stop or isolate the relevant activity first. Submit facts, impacts, and unresolved questions to an authorized person for confirmation before continuing.

Practical entry point: entry-level media technical director/manager samples use only public or fictional data to demonstrate equipment testing, switching, and compliance judgments. First confirm the role's first-year tasks and review methods.

O*NET respondents' education for this US suboccupation: 92% bachelor's degrees, 4% high school, and 1% postsecondary certificates. JobZone4 describes general preparation, not a uniform threshold or Chinese requirement. Chinese production and operation permits concern organizations conducting specified business, distinct from individual appointments, training, and material copyright.

Paper portfolio: this page's 30-minute, three-segment switching plan, five equipment prechecks, two escalations for C2's fault and P1's permission, approved conditional branches, one correction, and evidence for continuing or stopping. Do not operate equipment or submit real programs or contracts.
Interviews and trials: demonstrate how you test equipment, switch and handle effects according to scripts, monitor broadcast compliance, and stop and escalate when anomalies occur.

Editorial seven-day plan (30—60 minutes daily on paper): Day 1, read the script and states. Day 2, independently calculate three segments and the dissolve. Day 3, list prechecks and permissions. Day 4, write two anomalies and conditional branches. Day 5, hide answers, recalculate, and correct errors. Day 6, have a peer check independently using only the problem statement. Day 7, compile records and evidence for continuing or stopping. No real equipment operation or broadcasting.

Separate organizational permits, individual appointments, and material copyright. Articles Two and Four of China's 2025 revised Provisions on the Administration of Radio and Television Program Production and Operation specify production and operation scope and organizational permits; Article Eleven exempts legally established radio and television stations from obtaining this additional permit. It is not an individual programming director license, a station establishment permit, or material authorization.

Capability ladder: before entering media technical direction/management, verify the official occupational scope, actual employer requirements, education or training, local rules, and supervised tasks. Do not infer these directly from adjacent occupations. Advancement rests on reviewable switching and test records, not a guaranteed number of years.

Transition path: before changing direction, list transferable skills in technical control, equipment testing, departmental coordination, and broadcast compliance, alongside policy, permission, and safety knowledge to acquire. Check each against adjacent roles' qualifications and responsibilities.

US parent occupation 27-2012: 181,000 employed in 2025, projected 188,300 in 2035, growth of 4% over 2025—2035, and net increase of 7,300; 12,100 average annual openings include replacements. Not media technical directors/managers separately, current recruitment, or individual success rates.
